newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's ex-PM more manager than politician.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's ex-PM more manager than politician.

text.p: Ukrainian Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, whose resignation was accepted by President Leonid Kuchma on Wednesday, sees himself as more of a manager than a politician.
During his 13 months in office, the former collective farm driver never spoke publicly on foreign policy issues or on problems in the political life of the country of 51 million.
Labelled by local media in Ukrainian as a "khazyayin" -- boss, or owner -- he once described himself as a "manager, not a politician".
Lazarenko, 44, has devoted his term in office to establishing order in certain, profitable spheres of the economy such as alcohol, tobacco, gas distribution and frequency market.
Lazarenko was named in May 1996 as Ukraine's fifth prime minister since independence from Moscow in 1991.

It was clear his grip on power was slipping when on June 19 Kuchma appointed a deputy prime minister as acting premier while Lazarenko himself was officially ill. His aides said, however, that he was feeling fine.
Since then Lazarenko has been a patient at an elite hospital near Kiev, but the nature of his ailment has been unclear.
Aides said he was exhausted. Doctors said he had severe varicose veins in the legs and was facing possible surgery.
Lazarenko comes from a rural family in the eastern industrial Dnipropetrovsk region.

His career initially followed a traditional Soviet-era path. He began as a driver at a collective farm. Soon, he was the boss, later rising to become governor of the region, one of Ukraine's most powerful financially and industrially.
The head of parliament's anti-corruption committee has accused him of giving a low-interest $11 million credit to a Dniprpetrovsk firm.

The New York Times recently quoted Western intelligence reports estimating Lazarenko had gained $200 million from unofficial involvement in United Energy Systems, which had a licence to import Russian gas and is Ukraine's biggest gas trader.
Lazarenko denied the charge.

"We have corruption in Ukraine as in any other country," he said in Canada in June. "Whether I am implicated in all these publications in the mass media, I'm telling you unambigously I am not implicated."

Lazarenko was behind a scheme introduced in 1995 which transferred distribution of imported Russian gas to a dozen private traders. Lazarenko defended the scheme, which he said helped slash state energy debts to Russia.

Critics of the scheme said traders did not pay all their taxes and that it helped bring about $2.2 billion in unpaid wages. Recently Kuchma and his top aides said it created a monopolistic, uncompetitive energy market.

Lazarenko said he had no plans to run in a presidential election in October 1999, but that he was "young and still had everything in front of him". He has said he would back Kuchma if he ran and tried to avoid open conflicts with him.
Lazarenko once said the ideal system for Ukraine would be a government headed by the leader of the party or group which won parliamentary elections.
He is close to several factions in the Verkhovna Rada or parliament. One faction, called Yednist (Unity) is composed almost exclusively of deputies elected in Dnipropetrovsk region.
Regional rivalries seemed to be highlighted last July when Lazarenko escaped an assassination attempt as his car was blown up on it way to Kiev airport.
Later he persuaded Kuchma to sack Donetsk's powerful governor, Volodymyr Shcherban, now leader of the Liberal Party of Ukraine, who was seen then as Lazarenko's personal rival.
Lazarenko speaks German and Russian, and is married with a son and two daughters.
